newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU rules old subsidies to SFP TV studios illegal.
newsitem.headline: EU rules old subsidies to SFP TV studios illegal.

text.p: The European Commission ruled on Wednesday that France had illegally granted 1.1 billion francs in subsidies to television programme producer Societe Francaise de Production (SFP) between 1993 and early 1996.
But bowing to a request by French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis the decision will not be made public before October 10, Commission officials said on Wednesday.
This is to allow for the French government to conclude the privatisation of the embattled company, the sources said.
"They want a fig leaf, they get a fig leaf," one source said.

It is unclear whether and when the money will have to be re-paid -- as it must under European Union rules banning state help if it does not ensure a company's viability and if it distorts competition.

That is because the Commission will likely have to re-open the case to examine any French state aid that is used to privatise and restructure the company, which has survived thanks to successive state-sponsored capital injections since the early 1990s, the sources said.
The French Finance Ministry announced on Monday that it had received three firm offers for SFP and that it would take a decision on the studio's privatisation by October 10.
Global Studios, headed by French businessman Walter Butler, has placed a bid for SFP but, according to press reports, wants a 1.2 billion franc state recapitalisation to cover restructuring.

SFP, the remains of the production arm of the former integrated French state broadcaster ORTF, has been under EU investigation since 1994 for unauthorised state capital injections and debt write-offs.

Although the Commission under EU rules must declare the past subsidies illegal, it apparently has some sympathy for the company's plight as it was never really given the chance to recover from its financial problems.

"The company has been running on state money without results...But there was never a restructuring plan," one source said, adding that French state-owned broadcasters, its main clients, had failed regularly to pay their bills.
"We are not closing the door on this. We do not exclude continue negotiating on a (fresh) restructuring plan," one source said.
